reason: The sources provide over 15 highly detailed, cross-verified claims about Magellan's construction, mission, and historic dive, making it excellent for a 45-second short.
story: To map Venus, NASA built a 'Frankenstein' spacecraft. Magellan was pieced together from leftover spare parts of the Voyager, Galileo, and Mariner 9 missions, including a recycled Voyager antenna. Launched in 1989 aboard Space Shuttle Atlantis, it became the first deep space probe deployed from a shuttle. Upon arriving at Venus in 1990, Magellan faced a world of crushing atmospheric pressure and temperatures reaching 475 degrees Celsius. Because Venus is perpetually cloaked in thick clouds, Magellan used synthetic aperture radar to pierce the haze. Over several 243-day cycles, it mapped an incredible 98% of the planet's surface, revealing a globally volcanic wasteland with no Earth-like plate tectonics and almost zero water erosion. In 1993, Magellan pioneered aerobraking to circularize its orbit. Finally, in October 1994, engineers commanded the probe to make a dramatic, intentional plunge into the Venusian atmosphere, gathering aerodynamic data before being vaporized.
angle: NASA built the highly successful Magellan spacecraft out of spare parts leftover from other famous missions like Voyager and Galileo, yet it still mapped 98% of Venus before its death dive.

claims.claim: The Magellan spacecraft was launched on May 4, 1989.
Magellan was the first deep space probe to be launched from a Space Shuttle.
Magellan was sent on its trajectory toward Venus using an Inertial Upper Stage booster.
To save costs, Magellan was built largely of spare parts leftover from other missions, including Voyager, Galileo, and Mariner 9.
Magellan's 3.7-meter high-gain antenna was a spare part leftover from the Voyager program.
The spacecraft was named in honor of the 16th-century Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan.
Magellan's launch was delayed by at least a year due to the 1986 Space Shuttle Challenger disaster.
Magellan arrived in orbit around Venus on August 10, 1990.
The thick, opaque clouds covering Venus required Magellan to use synthetic aperture radar rather than optical imaging to map the surface.
Each mapping cycle lasted 243 Earth days, which is the time it takes for Venus to rotate once.
Magellan's radar successfully mapped 98% of the Venusian surface.
Magellan's data revealed that at least 85% of Venus's surface is covered with volcanic flows.
Data from the spacecraft showed that Venus does not have Earth-like plate tectonics or continental drift.
The extreme lack of water on Venus means that surface erosion is an incredibly slow process.
Venus has extreme surface conditions with temperatures around 475 degrees Celsius and atmospheric pressure around 92 atmospheres.
Magellan successfully used an aerobraking method—using the planet's atmosphere to slow down—to circularize its orbit.
The mission ended in October 1994 when controllers commanded Magellan to plunge into the Venusian atmosphere.

disputed: The exact date of communication loss and destruction: S1 and S2 record that final contact was lost on October 13, 1994, while S5 and S6 date the signal loss to October 12, 1994, with the final loss of the spacecraft occurring on October 13. The script should attribute this timeline carefully or generally state 'mid-October 1994'.

Radar imaging resolution: Wording varies on the design target versus the actual processed resolution, ranging from 120-300 meters (S2) to 75 meters per pixel (S3, S5). The script should state the final resolution was roughly 75 to 100 meters.
